title: Why they studied the sky
hookLine: prayer times, the qiblah and the new moon made astronomy a devotion

lines: A MONTH THAT STARTS WITH A CRESCENT.
cards: The prayers come through the day, but when, exactly? Not by a clock on the wall. By the sun.
The Qur'an puts it plainly, in Pickthall's translation: "worship at fixed hours hath been enjoined on the believers." Fixed hours, read from shadows, from sunset, from the last light in the west.
Then a direction to face, from wherever you stand. Then a month that begins only when someone sees a thin crescent after sunset. Questions about the sky, and not idle ones.
They come from the prayer mat and the fast.

teach.b: Start with the moon. People asked the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, about the new moons, and the Qur'an answers, in Pickthall's words: "They are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage."
The crescent opens each month, so it opens Ramadan, the pilgrimage season and the feasts.

Bukhari records the Prophet's instruction: fast when you see it, stop fasting when you see it again, and if clouds hide it, complete the month as thirty days. The calendar rests on a human eye, looking west at dusk.

teach.h: TURN YOUR FACE, WHEREVER YOU ARE.
teach.b: The Qur'an tells believers to turn their faces toward the Sacred Mosque wherever they are. Near Mecca, you can almost point. Far away, on a round earth, finding that line takes geometry: angles and distances.

teach.h: SHADOWS AND SUNSETS MARK THE HOURS.
ONE HADITH, SEVERAL WAYS TO SIGHT.
teach.b: Tirmidhi records a report in which the angel Gabriel leads the Prophet in prayer at set moments: when the sun passes its height, when a shadow has grown, when the sun goes down, when the twilight fades.
Each is something you see in the sky or on the ground. So the astrolabe makers you met yesterday were working on questions that started at the mosque door.

The conversation hasn't stopped. Muslims today settle the new moon in more than one way: some communities wait for a sighting in their own sky, some accept a sighting from another country, and some rely on calculation.
Each reads the Prophet's instruction in its own way, and each is trying to keep the same fast.

how: Muslims begin Ramadan and the other months by the new crescent, set prayer times by the sun's position, and face the qiblah toward Mecca; communities differ on whether the crescent must be seen locally or may be accepted from elsewhere or by calculation.

o: the star map that desert travelers steered by
appointed times: the fixed hours set for prayer
the twelve lunar months of the Muslim year

s: the Qur'an ties the new moons to the pilgrimage
"they are fixed seasons for mankind and for the pilgrimage" (2:189, Pickthall).
Muslims all settle the new moon the same way
some wait for a local sighting, some accept a sighting from elsewhere, and some rely on calculation.
the prayer times were fixed by the clock
they are read from the sun: its height, a shadow's length, sunset and the fading of twilight.

games.q: it's the evening the month might end. you're looking west, and clouds cover the whole sky. nobody can see the crescent. what does the hadith say to do?
o: complete the month as thirty days.
wait, however long it takes, until someone sees it.
games.why: Bukhari records the Prophet's instruction: if the crescent is hidden from you, complete the month as thirty days. the calendar waits on the eye, but it doesn't wait forever.

practice: A new crescent shows low and thin in the west, just after sunset. Notice the light around you: how bright it is, which way the shadows fall, how long they are, the very things people read the hour from.
If you pray, you can let this quiet be part of waiting for the next prayer; if not, just keep watching the light.

wordCard.voice: Mawaqit, appointed times: the Qur'an's word for the fixed hours of prayer, one of the sky questions, with the direction of prayer and the new moon, that sent people to the stars. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: appointed times, the word Pickthall renders "fixed seasons" in 2:189.

carryVoice: Your line: science for prayer. The questions started at the mosque door. That's day nine hundred twenty-seven.
